output.query: calcified neurocysticercosis and epilepsy; antiseizure medication levels in pregnancy

results.finding: Patients with only calcified parenchymal cysticerci and seizures should not receive antiparasitic drugs; antiseizure medication is managed as in other epilepsies. Serum antibody tests are often negative with single or only calcified lesions.
results.source: White AC Jr et al., Clin Infect Dis 2018;66:e49-e75 | Diagnosis and treatment of neurocysticercosis: 2017 clinical practice guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH)

results.finding: Calcified cysticerci are a frequent cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions; perilesional edema around calcifications can recur and an association with hippocampal sclerosis has been described.
results.source: Garcia HH, Nash TE, Del Brutto OH, Lancet Neurol 2014;13:1202-1215 | Clinical symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment of neurocysticercosis

results.finding: Pregnancy may lower levetiracetam concentrations (Level C) and monitoring of its levels may be considered; lamotrigine, phenytoin and carbamazepine levels fall more consistently (Level B).
results.source: Harden CL et al., Neurology 2009;73:142-149 | Practice parameter update: management issues for women with epilepsy, focus on pregnancy: vitamin K, folic acid, blood levels, and breastfeeding

results.finding: Major congenital malformation rates were lowest with levetiracetam and low-dose lamotrigine monotherapy and highest with valproate, with a dose-dependent risk for most drugs.
results.source: Tomson T et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:530-538 | Comparative risk of major congenital malformations with eight different antiepileptic drugs: a prospective cohort study of the EURAP registry

output.summary: Guidelines advise against antiparasitic treatment when cysticerci are only calcified and note low serological sensitivity in that stage. In pregnancy, levels of several antiseizure medications fall, more consistently for lamotrigine than for levetiracetam, and registry data show the lowest malformation rates with levetiracetam and low-dose lamotrigine.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not switch to or add valproate: it is avoided in pregnancy because of its malformation and neurodevelopmental risks, and levetiracetam is effective when taken.
Do not delay obstetric and fetal assessment pending the neurological work-up.
Do not give gadolinium in pregnancy: it does not change management here.
Do not give albendazole or praziquantel: calcified neurocysticercosis needs no antiparasitic treatment, and albendazole is avoided in pregnancy.
required_recommendations: Arrange urgent obstetric and fetal assessment (fetal heart rate monitoring, maternal-fetal medicine) after the convulsion, and treat any new hypertension or proteinuria as eclampsia with magnesium sulfate.
Restart levetiracetam at once and increase the dose (for example to 750-1000 mg twice daily) to offset third-trimester clearance, guided by trough levels.
Plan to reduce the levetiracetam dose toward the pre-pregnancy dose over the first weeks after delivery to avoid toxicity.
Arrange social work support and a reliable levetiracetam supply (refills, coverage, a single pharmacy) given homelessness and missed doses.
Advise on newborn safety: breastfeeding is compatible with levetiracetam; feed sitting supported, change the baby on the floor and bathe the baby only with another adult present.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism, back to baseline and immunocompetent; a breakthrough seizure after missed doses gives no indication for lumbar puncture in late pregnancy.
The event began with her habitual deja vu aura and was a witnessed convulsion with prolonged confusion; nothing suggests structural heart disease.
No syncope-versus-seizure question remains: aura, stare, convulsion and 20 minutes of confusion are epileptic, and the ECG is normal.

Gadolinium crosses the placenta and gestational exposure is linked to stillbirth or neonatal death and inflammatory skin conditions; it adds nothing to characterizing calcified lesions and hippocampal sclerosis.
FDG-PET exposes the fetus to radiation and adds nothing to a diagnosis made by concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy, not pregnancy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with mesial temporal sclerosis, secondary to remote calcified neurocysticercosis (dual pathology), presenting at 33 weeks gestation

differential.key_features: A convulsion at 33 weeks must be treated as eclampsia until excluded; blood pressure 112/68, urine protein/creatinine 0.11, normal platelets, creatinine and liver enzymes exclude it.
Viable cysts would need antiparasitic decisions; MRI shows only calcified nodules without cyst, scolex or edema.
Other causes of healed calcified granulomas; QuantiFERON and HIV are negative and the pattern of small cortical-subcortical calcifications fits neurocysticercosis in a patient from rural Guatemala.
The shelter called it syncope and earlier events were labelled vasovagal, but a deja vu aura, 60 seconds of convulsion and 20 minutes of confusion are epileptic; the ECG is normal.
Stereotyped deja vu and epigastric auras, right temporal sharp waves and right hippocampal sclerosis make PNES unlikely.

differential.diagnosis: Hyponatremia or another metabolic provoked seizure
differential.key_features: Sodium, glucose, calcium and magnesium are normal.

key_clinical_evidence: A convulsion at 33 weeks requires exclusion of eclampsia; normal blood pressure, urine protein/creatinine, platelets, creatinine and liver enzymes exclude it.

Years of stereotyped deja vu and epigastric rising auras meet the definition of epilepsy; this convulsion is a breakthrough seizure after missed doses with a low levetiracetam level in late pregnancy.
Right anterior temporal sharp waves on EEG and right hippocampal sclerosis on MRI localize the epilepsy to the right mesial temporal lobe.

Multiple calcified nodules without cyst or edema in a patient from rural Guatemala indicate calcified neurocysticercosis; a negative serum cysticercosis IgG does not exclude it, and calcified lesions need no antiparasitic treatment.
Levetiracetam clearance rises in pregnancy and falls after delivery, so the dose is raised now and reduced after delivery.
Homelessness and interrupted medication supply caused the breakthrough and must be addressed for seizure control.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

Ventricles normal in size; no hydrocephalus.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Coyoy is a 31-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman at 33 weeks of gestation who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed syncopal episode at a homeless shelter. Shelter staff report that the patient was sitting at a table when she suddenly stopped talking and appeared to stare blankly for approximately 10 seconds. She then developed stiffening of her upper extremities followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs lasting approximately 60 seconds. She was placed on her left side by shelter staff during the episode. Afterward, she was confused and unable to answer questions for approximately 20 minutes before gradually returning to her baseline. Upon interview through a Spanish interpreter, the patient recalls experiencing a strong sense of familiarity, as if she had lived through that moment before, accompanied by a rising sensation in her stomach just before losing awareness. She reports a history of similar brief episodes of intense deja vu with an epigastric rising sensation occurring two to three times per month over the past several years, each lasting approximately 30 to 60 seconds, after which she feels briefly disoriented. She was diagnosed with epilepsy approximately 10 years ago following the birth of her first child and was started on levetiracetam at that time. She reports inconsistent access to her medication since arriving in the United States and estimates she has missed several doses over the past two weeks due to difficulty obtaining refills. She also reports a headache that began approximately two hours after the event, described as bilateral, dull, and rated 4 out of 10 in severity. She denies nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, fever, chills, visual changes, weight loss, or any new focal weakness. She denies any recent head trauma, illness, or changes in medications other than the missed doses. She reports no complications with her current pregnancy and states her prenatal care has been followed at a community health clinic. In Guatemala, the first events after the birth of her first child were initially attributed to vasovagal syncope before epilepsy was diagnosed.
